body_text: A measles outbreak in Majorca has prompted health authorities to intensify surveillance and contact tracing after six cases were identified in the Balearic Islands. The outbreak has attracted particular attention because Majorca is a major international holiday destination, welcoming large numbers of visitors during the summer season. Health officials are now working to identify people who may have been exposed to the virus, including passengers who travelled on flights connected with the investigation. According to reports published on August 10, 2026, Spain's health authorities confirmed six measles cases in the Balearic Islands. Five of the six people were reportedly unvaccinated, while the vaccination status of the remaining person was not known. Although none of those affected have required hospitalisation, officials are warning that additional cases could emerge because measles is highly contagious and can spread rapidly among people who do not have immunity. How the Majorca measles outbreak began Health officials have traced the beginning of the outbreak to a child who was visiting Majorca from another European country. The child attended the Paediatric Emergency Service at Son Espases hospital in Palma on July 19. Investigators subsequently identified other linked cases and began examining possible routes of transmission. Authorities have stressed that the hospital itself has not been identified as the source of the outbreak. Instead, the cases are being investigated as part of community transmission. The timing of the investigation is significant because measles can remain unnoticed for a period before symptoms become obvious. People can also be infectious before the characteristic rash appears, making contact tracing particularly important. Health authorities have therefore activated surveillance and contact tracing procedures to identify people who may have been exposed. Tourists may be contacted as part of the investigation One of the biggest challenges for officials is determining how widely the virus may have travelled. Majorca attracts visitors from across Europe and beyond, meaning a person exposed on the island could return home before developing symptoms. Authorities are consequently investigating travel and flight connections linked to the outbreak. People identified as potentially exposed may receive text messages advising them to check their vaccination status and monitor themselves for symptoms. Reports indicate that people considered at risk may be asked to remain alert for symptoms for up to 23 days following exposure. This reflects the relatively long period between infection and the development of symptoms in some measles cases. The investigation could involve a significant number of people because international travel creates numerous potential contacts. Why measles spreads so easily Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. It spreads primarily through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. People without immunity can become infected after exposure, particularly in crowded environments such as airports, aircraft, public transport, schools and healthcare facilities. The disease typically begins with symptoms such as fever, tiredness, cough, a runny nose and red or watery eyes. A distinctive rash usually develops several days later and can spread from the face and head across the body. Because the early symptoms can resemble those of other viral infections, people may not immediately realise they have measles. This is one reason vaccination remains an important tool for preventing outbreaks. Vaccination remains the main protection The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, commonly known as the MMR vaccine, provides protection against measles. Spain's Ministry of Health recommends two doses of the combined vaccine as part of routine childhood vaccination. The country's health authorities state that more than 95 percent of the population has received the first dose and around 94 percent has received the second dose, according to vaccination information updated in 2025. The Balearic Islands have also reported high vaccination coverage, although the coverage cited in reports about the current outbreak is below the level generally considered necessary to prevent sustained transmission. The current outbreak highlights the importance of maintaining strong vaccination coverage, particularly in communities with frequent international travel. People who are unsure whether they have received the recommended doses should check their vaccination records and speak with a qualified healthcare professional if they need advice. What are the symptoms of measles? Recognising possible symptoms is important, especially for people who have recently travelled to or from an area where measles cases have been reported. Common symptoms can include: High fever Cough Runny nose Red or watery eyes General tiredness Small white spots inside the mouth A red or brownish rash that usually begins around the head and spreads across the body The illness can sometimes lead to serious complications. These may include pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, inflammation of the brain and problems affecting vision. Young children, pregnant people and individuals with weakened immune systems can be particularly vulnerable to complications. Anyone who develops symptoms after a possible exposure should seek medical advice and mention the potential measles exposure before visiting a healthcare facility in person. This allows healthcare workers to take appropriate precautions and reduce the risk of exposing other patients. Should tourists cancel trips to Majorca? The discovery of an outbreak does not automatically mean that every visitor to Majorca is at significant risk. The level of risk depends on several factors, including vaccination status, age, health circumstances and whether someone has had close contact with an infected person. However, the situation is a reminder that travellers should check their routine vaccinations before international holidays. People planning to travel with children should ensure their vaccinations are up to date where appropriate. Adults who are uncertain about their vaccination history can also speak with a healthcare professional before travelling. Travel-related outbreaks can be difficult to contain because infected individuals may move between countries during the period before symptoms become obvious. This makes vaccination and early recognition particularly important. Officials expect further monitoring Health authorities have indicated that additional cases are possible as investigations continue. The six confirmed cases are being monitored, while affected individuals have been instructed to isolate at home. Authorities are continuing to identify potential contacts and assess possible routes of transmission. The Majorca outbreak is also taking place against a wider backdrop of increasing measles activity in Spain and internationally. Spain had previously maintained measles elimination status, meaning sustained endemic transmission had been interrupted. Recent increases in cases have nevertheless created renewed public health concerns. For holidaymakers, the key message is not to panic but to stay informed. Checking vaccination records, understanding the symptoms of measles and following advice from local health authorities can all help reduce the risk of further transmission. Majorca remains a popular destination for international travellers, but the current outbreak demonstrates why infectious diseases can quickly cross borders in a highly connected world. Final thoughts The measles outbreak in Majorca has triggered an extensive public health response, with officials working to identify potentially exposed tourists and other contacts. Six cases have been confirmed so far, with most of those affected reportedly having no documented measles vaccination. While none of the confirmed patients has required hospitalisation, authorities are continuing to monitor the situation and have warned that more infections could be identified. For travellers, vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect against measles. Anyone who believes they may have been exposed should monitor for symptoms and seek professional medical advice. The situation may change as health authorities continue their investigation, so travellers should rely on official health guidance for the latest information. Source The Sun on August 10, 2026. Disclaimer This article is provided for general information and news reporting purposes only. It is not medical advice, a diagnosis or a substitute for consultation with a qualified healthcare professional. Health guidance and outbreak information can change as investigations develop. Anyone concerned about measles exposure, vaccination or symptoms should contact an appropriate healthcare professional or local health authority for personalised advice.

title: Xcel Energy invites volunteers to its 16th annual Day of Service
summary: Xcel Energy invites the public to join employees and their friends and family on Thursday, September 10 through Saturday, September 12 for its 16th annual Day of Service, an opportunity to give back to their communities.
body_text: DENVER (Aug. 5, 2026) — Xcel Energy invites the public to join employees and their friends and family on Thursday, September 10 through Saturday, September 12 for its 16th annual Day of Service, an opportunity to give back to their communities. Volunteers can sign up now for one of more than 40 nonprofit projects in Colorado. Many are based in the Denver metro area, with other opportunities in Grand Junction, Alamosa, Pueblo and Fort Collins. Indoor and outdoor projects are available and include land stewardship; packing and serving meals for those with food insecurities; and cleaning and organizing nonprofit storage spaces. “Day of Service is one of the most meaningful ways we live our commitment to the communities we serve,” said Robert Kenney, president, Xcel Energy – Colorado. “One of the things that makes our communities so strong is people’s willingness to help one another, and we’re proud to give our time and resources to support our neighbors and local nonprofits. We invite people of all ages and abilities to join us in giving back and helping strengthen the places we proudly call home.” Xcel Energy’s Day of Service has been an annual tradition since 2010 and is the company’s largest volunteer effort. Last year, more than 2,900 employees, contractors, friends, family, retirees and customers across the eight states Xcel Energy serves contributed 8,890 hours, including packing 81,600 meals and assembling 6,600 kits for teachers and students. Their efforts benefited nearly 100 nonprofits and generated an economic impact of more than $321,000. Day of Service was created as a tribute to the victims, survivors and first responders of 9/11, as well as all those who work to keep communities and the country safe. The annual volunteer event provides an opportunity for Xcel Energy and members of the community to come together and contribute to projects that benefit local nonprofits. People of all ages and abilities can participate. Learn more about Day of Service and sign up for a volunteer project through this link . Registration closes on August 28. # # # About Xcel Energy Xcel Energy (NASDAQ: XEL) is a leading energy provider, dedicated to serving millions of customers with excellence. We make energy work better for customers, helping them thrive every day. That means always raising the bar — delivering better service and providing more reliable, resilient and sustainable energy. We are committed to leading the clean energy transition, meeting our customers’ need for more, cleaner power, while keeping bills as low as possible. Because the people we serve depend on us to power their lives. Headquartered in Minneapolis, we work every day to generate and distribute electricity and gas to customers across eight states: Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas. For more information, visit xcelenergy.com or follow us on X and Facebook .

title: The LinkedIn Buzzwords Recruiters Skip Right Past (and What to Write Instead)
summary: Passionate, results-driven, Growth Ninja: the LinkedIn buzzwords recruiters skim past, why they fail search, and the concrete words to write instead.
body_text: Which LinkedIn buzzwords do recruiters skip, and what should you write instead? Passionate, results-driven, detail-oriented, self-starter, thought leader, plus titles like Growth Ninja. A recruiter skims past all of them, because everyone types them and no one can verify them. Then there is the mechanical problem. These are not search terms, so a headline built on adjectives never surfaces when a recruiter runs their search. The fix is to swap them for your plain job title, your real skills, and one result you can point to. "Senior Data Analyst | SQL + Python | dashboards that cut churn" gets read. "Passionate problem-solver driving synergy" gets scrolled. Open your LinkedIn headline and read it out loud. Right now. If that line could sit under forty thousand other names without anyone noticing, you have found the problem. Take results-driven professional passionate about driving cross-functional synergy . A recruiter reads maybe the first four words and moves on, the same way you skate past a cookie banner. And here is what makes it almost funny. We can all spot how empty this stuff is on someone else's profile. Then we open our own headline field and type the exact same words. This is not a style complaint. Buzzwords fail on LinkedIn for two mechanical reasons, and each one quietly costs you a recruiter's attention. So let's pull the language apart, figure out where it does the most damage, and rebuild it into something a recruiter can actually find and believe. Why buzzwords carry zero signal A word earns its place when it sets you apart from the next candidate in the list. "Passionate" does the reverse. Picture a recruiter with thirty tabs open, every single one claiming to be passionate, driven, and detail-oriented. At that point the words are wallpaper. The brain stops reading them. By the twelfth profile before lunch, a recruiter filters that whole vocabulary out and does not even clock that they did. The deeper problem is that these are self-claims nobody can check. Anyone can type "strong leader" into their about section between meetings. The word costs nothing and proves nothing, so an experienced reader discounts it on sight. It is the same flaw that sinks a bare list of soft skills on a resume: you have asserted a trait and handed the reader no reason to believe it. Hiring teams want evidence. An adjective is the absence of evidence, dressed up to pass as a qualification. LinkedIn has been saying as much for over a decade. Every year from 2010 to 2018 the company put out a roundup of the profile words its members overused the most. The 2017 list, to give you the flavor, was topped by "Specialized" and "Leadership," with "Passionate" at number three and "Strategic," "Experienced," and "Expert" close behind. A few of them, "Strategic" and "Creative" and "Expert," turned up almost every single year. LinkedIn quietly dropped the annual list after 2018. Its advice from back then still lands, though: your achievements beat any generic adjective. Show the reader what you did, and the adjective stops being necessary at all. The headline is where it hurts most Of all the places a buzzword can hide, the headline is the worst spot for it. Here is why. That line is roughly 220 characters, and it follows you absolutely everywhere on the platform. Under your name in search results. Beside every comment you leave. Inside the little hover-preview a recruiter reads before deciding to click through or scroll on. And on a phone, only the first sixty or seventy characters even render, which means your opening words are doing almost the entire job. Now picture that line reading Innovative Leader | Passionate Problem-Solver | Driving Impact . You have spent your single most valuable piece of real estate on four words that mean nothing and one that means less. A recruiter scanning a list of thirty candidates gets no information from it. They cannot tell what you do, what you specialize in, or whether you are a fit for the role open on their desk. So they keep scrolling. The headline sits right beside your photo in that preview, and if you are working on the visual first impression too, your profile photo is the other half of that same split-second judgment. Now the same slot built out of facts: Senior Data Analyst | SQL + Python | dashboards that cut SaaS churn . One glance, and a recruiter has your level, your two core tools, and a real outcome. Searchable. Scannable. Specific. That is the entire job of a headline, and no quantity of "passionate" gets you any of it. Recruiters search, they don't scroll Here is the mechanical reason buzzwords fail, and it is the one most people never think about. Recruiters almost never discover candidates by browsing. They fill roles by searching. A recruiter with a data-analyst requisition opens LinkedIn Recruiter and types a query built from a job title, a couple of skills, and a location. The system hands back the profiles whose text contains those terms. If your profile does not carry the words the recruiter typed, you never load into the results at all. Adjectives are not the words recruiters type. Nobody has ever searched "passionate." Nobody filters a candidate pool by "results-driven" or "go-getter." What they type is "financial analyst," or "Kubernetes," or "registered nurse," or "Series A." Job titles, hard skills, tools. That is the vocabulary the search runs on, and buzzwords are simply invisible to it. So a profile written entirely in self-describing adjectives is unfindable in the most literal sense. You could be the strongest candidate on the market and still never surface on a single recruiter's screen. This is the part people underrate, because it happens silently. You do not get a rejection. You get nothing, and you assume the market is dead or your background is weak, when the real issue is that your profile is written in a language the search engine does not read. We go deep on exactly how that search works in this breakdown of why recruiters never message you on LinkedIn , and the short version is simple: the headline and the skills section are search fields first and personality statements a distant second. The worst offenders, grouped into a cut-list Not all buzzwords fail the same way. It helps to sort them into three buckets, because each one needs a slightly different fix. Use this as a scan, not a scripture. If a word describes something you can prove with a fact, it can stay. If it is just decoration, cut it. Bucket one is the empty adjectives. Passionate, results-driven, detail-oriented, hardworking, motivated, dynamic, self-starter, go-getter, team player, strategic, innovative. Pure self-claims, all of them. They announce what you would like a reader to believe about you and offer nothing to back it up. Delete each one, or replace it with the fact that would make a stranger reach that conclusion without being told. Then the novelty titles. Growth Ninja, Sales Rockstar, Marketing Guru, Code Wizard, Chief Happiness Officer, Brand Evangelist. Inside a scrappy startup these can be genuinely affectionate, and the appeal is real. On LinkedIn they cost you twice over. Nobody searches "ninja," so the title disappears from recruiter search entirely. And for most serious roles it reads as unserious the instant a hiring manager sees it. If the whimsical title is the real one on your badge, keep it, but bolt the plain version on beside it so the search can still find you. Last comes the corporate jargon : synergy, thought leadership, leveraging, holistic, cross-functional, disruptor, change-maker, visionary, moving the needle, boiling the ocean. This is the language of the internal all-hands leaking onto a public page. It signals that you are fluent in meetings, not that you are good at the job, and plenty of readers find it actively grating. Swap it for a plain description of what you actually do. Show, don't tell: prove the trait instead of claiming it The single most useful move in this whole makeover is to quit claiming traits and start proving them. That sounds abstract. Make it concrete. The word "leadership" sitting in your about section persuades exactly no one. But a line that says you ran a team of six through a billing-platform migration with no missed deadlines? That persuades everyone, and it never once uses the word "leadership." The reader draws the conclusion on their own, and that is the only version that sticks. Every buzzword has a stronger, provable replacement hiding behind it. "Detail-oriented" becomes "reconciled month-end accounts across four entities with zero audit adjustments." "Results-driven" becomes "grew trial-to-paid conversion from 8 percent to 14 percent in two quarters." "Excellent communicator" becomes "wrote the onboarding docs the whole support team now trains from." Notice that none of the replacements are adjectives. They are all small facts, and a fact does the persuading that an adjective only gestures at. This is the same trap that sinks resumes, which is why the buzzwords that clutter resumes are worth cutting on both surfaces at once. If you have ever struggled with this because your work does not come with obvious metrics, you are not stuck. Concrete does not have to mean numeric. Scope, frequency, firsts, and before-and-after states all count, and we walk through the whole method in this guide to quantifying achievements when you have no numbers . The principle is the same on LinkedIn as it is on a resume: a specific replaces a buzzword, and it always wins. Is your headline working, or just filling the space? Get a free LinkedIn review that flags the buzzwords, the missing keywords, and the vague about opener a recruiter skims past. Review my LinkedIn → The about opener: swap the cliche first line The about section has its own version of the headline problem, and it lives in the first sentence. LinkedIn only shows the opening line or two before the "see more" cutoff, so that first line is a second headline whether you meant it to be or not. Most people waste it. They open with something like I am a passionate professional dedicated to delivering value and driving results across dynamic, fast-paced environments. A reader learns nothing and clicks away. Open with a fact instead. Name what you do and one thing that makes you specifically worth the recruiter's next thirty seconds. "I build the data pipelines that keep a 200-person sales org running on numbers it can trust" tells a stranger more than three paragraphs of adjectives. The rest of the section then becomes proof: a short run of concrete accomplishments, each one demonstrating a trait you would otherwise have been tempted to just claim. Treat the about section as a pitch answering one question, why you for this kind of role right now, rather than a diary of where you have been. If the whole about-section structure is what you are stuck on, that is the place to start after you have fixed the opener. Novelty titles: cute until a recruiter searches Novelty titles deserve their own section because people defend them the hardest. The instinct is understandable. A "Growth Ninja" title feels like personality in a sea of sameness, and if your company genuinely gave you that title, throwing it away feels dishonest. Here is the resolution: you do not have to throw it away, you have to translate it. These titles hurt for reasons that have nothing to do with fun. Search is the first one. A recruiter who needs a growth marketer types "growth marketer," and "Growth Ninja" is not a match, full stop. You tuned the title for a laugh and detuned it for the one system that decides whether anyone finds you. Notice a second pattern while you are at it. You almost never see a senior role dressed up this way. There is no "CFO Wizard." Novelty titles pile up at the junior end, where they puff a smaller role into something bigger, and that inflation is exactly the read you do not want landing on a hiring manager's screen. So keep the flavor, just add the function next to it. "Growth Ninja (Growth Marketing Manager)" hands the search engine its term and lets you keep the personality. "Chief Happiness Officer | Head of People Ops" does the same. You lose nothing and you become findable. One caveat by field: in finance, law, healthcare, or government, drop the novelty entirely and lead with the plain title. Whimsy that charms at a Series A startup reads as a red flag to a compliance-heavy employer. The 2026 twist: buzzwords now read as AI slop There is a newer reason to cut the buzzwords, and it has nothing to do with the old cliche fatigue. A profile that is all confident adjectives and no specifics now trips a different alarm in the reader's head: this was written by a chatbot. Think about what raw AI output actually sounds like. Dense with buzzwords. Light on proof. Relentlessly upbeat. That is the exact texture of a headline stuffed with "visionary" and "results-driven" and "passionate about driving impact." A recruiter clocks it in a second and files the whole profile under "generated," which is a worse verdict than plain old generic. The fix is the same as it was before AI existed, which is the reassuring part. Concrete nouns, real specifics, and actual proof read as human because a machine reaching for the statistically safe phrase does not produce them. If you want the full field guide to the tells, from the "not X, but Y" cadence to the em-dash density, we cover them in this piece on how AI-written LinkedIn profiles hurt you . Buzzwords and AI slop are two names for the same underlying failure: language that says a lot and proves nothing. The exception that proves the rule: "Ex-Google" One headline tactic genuinely works, and it is worth a look because a single word explains the whole principle. Drop "Ex-Google" or "Ex-Stripe" into your headline, or the name of any company a recruiter recognizes, and the number of people reaching out goes up. At a glance that looks like a buzzword. A bit of name-dropping. It is not, and the reason it is not is the entire point of this article. "Ex-Google" pulls its weight because it is concrete, checkable, and searchable. A recruiter can verify it in one click. It signals a real bar you cleared. And it is a term people actually type into the filter. Compare that to "passionate," which is checkable by no one and searched by no one. So the takeaway is not "go add company names." The rule underneath is bigger than that: the phrases that draw recruiters in are the ones a stranger can verify and search for, and the phrases they skip are the ones you could paste onto anybody's profile. You can watch that same rule play out at every stage in this walkthrough of how hiring really works . A before-and-after makeover Put it all together and the before-and-after is stark. Start with the headline as most people write it: Dynamic, results-driven marketing professional | Passionate storyteller | Thought leader driving synergy and impact . That is a hundred-odd characters of nothing. No role to search. No skill. No proof. And in 2026 it carries that faint whiff of machine-written text on top of everything else. Now the same person after: Content Marketing Manager | SEO + lifecycle email | grew organic signups 3x in 18 months . Every element earns its place. "Content Marketing Manager" is the searchable title. "SEO" and "lifecycle email" are the skills a recruiter filters for. "Grew organic signups 3x in 18 months" is the proof that replaces every adjective the old version was leaning on. It is shorter, it is findable, and it makes a claim a stranger has a reason to believe. The about opener gets the same treatment. Before: I am a passionate marketer dedicated to excellence. After: I turn early-stage products into repeatable inbound channels, most recently taking a B2B SaaS from 400 to 1,200 organic signups a month. Same person, same career. One version is skimmed past and one is read, and the only thing that changed was trading claims for facts. The fill-in replacement formula If you want a repeatable way to rebuild your own profile, use this. For the headline: plain job title, then one or two real skills or tools, then one concrete result or specialty. Separate the parts with a pipe so the eye can scan them. Front-load the title, because the first sixty characters are what shows in previews. Skip every adjective; if you feel the urge to type "experienced," put the years or the scope instead. For the about opener: one sentence naming what you do and who you do it for, then one specific that proves you are good at it. No "passionate," no "dedicated," no "dynamic." Then let the body of the section carry three or four accomplishments that each demonstrate a trait you would otherwise have claimed. The same show-don't-tell logic governs where and how you present skills more broadly, which we get into in this guide to the skills section , and it is worth reading alongside this because a headline and a skills list are solving the same search-and-proof problem. Run the whole profile through one final test before you call it done. Cover every proper noun, number, and tool with your thumb. If what remains could describe literally anyone in your field, you have written buzzwords. Put the specifics back, and make sure the sentences between them could only have been written about you. That is the line between a profile a recruiter skips and one they open. Frequently Asked Questions What are the worst LinkedIn buzzwords to avoid? The ones that describe you and prove nothing. Passionate. Results-driven. Detail-oriented. Self-starter, go-getter, team player, dynamic, motivated, hardworking, strategic. Add the corporate set on top of that: synergy, thought leader, visionary, change-maker. Then the novelty titles, Growth Ninja and Marketing Guru and the rest. LinkedIn ran its own annual roundup of these from 2010 through 2018, and "passionate" and "strategic" were near-permanent fixtures. But do not memorize a banned list. Just ask one thing of every word: can I back this with a fact? No? Cut it. Why do recruiters ignore buzzword-heavy profiles? One human reason, one mechanical. The human one: everyone writes the same adjectives, so they stop telling anybody apart, and a recruiter trains themselves to skim right over them. The mechanical one is worse. Recruiters find people by searching, and they search job titles, skills, and tools, never adjectives. So a profile built on buzzwords does not appear in their results at all. Honestly, "ignore" is too kind a word. Half the time your profile was never even seen, because the terms a recruiter typed were nowhere on your page. What should I put in my LinkedIn headline instead? Plain job title first. Then one or two of the real tools or skills you use. Then one concrete result or focus. Something like "Financial Analyst | Excel + SQL | built the forecast model for a $40M P&L." Front-load the title, because only the first sixty-odd characters show in search previews and on mobile. You get about 220 characters in total. The opening words carry the weight, so do not burn them on "innovative" or "dynamic." Are novelty job titles like "Growth Ninja" bad on LinkedIn? For getting found, yes. Nobody searches "ninja," so the title vanishes from the search that decides whether you turn up. For most roles it also reads as unserious the moment a hiring manager lands on it, and it tends to sit on junior positions where it puffs up the level. Here is the thing though: if your company actually handed you that title, do not bin it. Translate it. Write "Growth Ninja (Growth Marketing Manager)." The search gets the real term. You keep the character. Do buzzwords hurt my searchability on LinkedIn? Less "hurt" than "waste," and the result is identical. Recruiters run keyword and Boolean searches across your title, skills, and headline. Adjectives are not search terms. So every character spent on one is a character not spent on a word that would have surfaced you. Think of it this way. Every "passionate" is a real keyword you traded away. Put the actual title, the tools, and the skills a recruiter would type back in, and you cross the line from invisible to visible in the only search that counts. How do I fix the first line of my LinkedIn about section? LinkedIn only shows the first line or two before the "see more" fold, so that opening sentence is basically a second headline. Kill the "I am a passionate professional dedicated to excellence" version. Swap in a fact: what you do, who you do it for, and one thing worth the reader's next thirty seconds. "I build the reporting a 200-person sales team trusts to make calls" beats any run of adjectives. It hands a stranger a reason to keep reading, which is the whole job of a first line. Does a strong LinkedIn profile guarantee recruiters will message me? No, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What you control is this: cutting the buzzwords and adding real keywords makes you findable and makes the first impression land. How much inbound actually shows up still depends on your field, your seniority, and how hot the market is that quarter. People in in-demand roles field messages weekly. People in flooded fields hear crickets no matter how clean the profile. Findable is not the same as flooded. The point here is to delete every reason a recruiter would skip you, not to promise a flood that no profile can. Is it true that buzzword profiles now look AI-written? More and more, yes. A headline or about section that is all confident adjectives and zero specifics reads exactly like raw chatbot output: fluent, upbeat, hollow. A recruiter sees "visionary leader passionate about driving impact" and a small part of their brain now files it under "generated," not "written." Bad look. And the fix is the same one that cured plain old cliche years ago: concrete nouns, real numbers, actual proof. We lay out the full set of tells in our guide to AI-written LinkedIn profiles . Should I ever keep a word like "strategic" or "expert"? Only if a fact follows it immediately. "Strategic" alone is filler. "Set the three-year data strategy that folded five tools into one platform" earns the idea and never needs the label. So the honest version is that you almost never keep the adjective. You keep the accomplishment that would have justified it. Cannot point to the thing behind the word? Then the word was decoration. And decoration is precisely what a recruiter skims past. Where do I find synonyms if I still want a punchier word? You can, and a sharper verb does sometimes make a bullet read better. Just do not mistake a thesaurus for the fix. Trade "passionate" for "dedicated" and you have changed the word, not the problem, because both are still self-claims nobody can verify. Want stronger phrasing? Start from the accomplishment, then pick a verb that names the action you actually took, using something like our list of resume action words . The verb has to attach to a real thing you did. It cannot float free as a label. title: Tailwinds for MIDD: What to Know About the Changing Regulatory Landscape
summary: FDA's evolving MIDD guidance is reshaping drug development. Join Certara's scientific leaders in Cambridge, MA for an interactive discussion on Sept 30
body_text: Share Share Share An exclusive in-person Certara roadshow Date: September 30, 2026 Time: 11:30 AM – 2:00 PM Location: CIC Cambridge, 1 Broadway, Cambridge, MA 02142 Regulators around the world are converging on the same conclusion: MIDD should be a core part of how evidence is built and evaluated across drug development. ICH M15 has established the first harmonized global framework for MIDD, and FDA’s Operation TrialBlazer guidances, including new recommendations for QSP-based dose selection in first-in-human trials, reflect a broader momentum toward formalizing modeling’s role in regulatory decision-making. Taken together, these developments signal growing confidence in MIDD approaches as trusted contributors to the evidence package, not just supporting analyses. This session brings together three of Certara’s most recognized scientific leaders across Quantitative Systems Pharmacology (QSP), Physiologically-Based Pharmacokinetics (PBPK), and Pharmacometrics for a candid, cross-disciplinary discussion on this momentum, and how sponsors can capitalize on it by building modeling strategies that give them the best chance of success with regulators. Register now Registrations are subject to review and approval What to expect Perspectives from Certara’s leading scientific voices across Pharmacometrics, MBMA, PBPK, and QSP A candid look at how FDA’s evolving guidance is redefining the role of MIDD in regulatory decision-making Practical strategies for integrating modeling disciplines into a single, defensible regulatory narrative An open, interactive Q&A designed for real dialogue Networking with experts and peers across clinical pharmacology, quantitative sciences, and regulatory strategy Speakers: Piet van der Graaf Senior Vice President and Head of Quantitative Systems Pharmacology Piet van der Graaf, PharmD, PhD is Senior Vice President Applied BioSimulation at Certara, Professor of Systems Pharmacology at Leiden University, and Professor of Pediatrics at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center. Previously, he was the Director of the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research and held leadership positions at Pfizer in Discovery Biology, DMPK and Clinical Pharmacology. He was the founding Editor-in-Chief of CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology before becoming Editor-in-Chief of Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics. Piet received his doctorate training in clinical medicine with Nobel prize laureate Sir James Black at King’s College London. He was awarded the 2024 Gary Neil Prize for Innovation in Drug Development from the American Society of Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics (ASCPT) and the 2021 Leadership Award from the International Society of Pharmacometrics (ISoP). Piet is an elected Fellow of the British Pharmacological Society and has published >250 articles in the area of quantitative pharmacology and drug development. Karen Rowland Yeo, PhD Senior Vice President, Client & Regulatory Strategy Karen is Senior Vice-President, Client & Regulatory Strategy at Certara UK Limited’s Simcyp Division. Prior to this, she was the Head of PBPK Consultancy Services at Simcyp where she led a team of scientists engaged in Consultancy projects relating to the application of physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling in drug development. Her work has focused on the use of PBPK models for assessment of drug-drug interactions and dosing of special populations and she is the author/co-author of more than 100 peer reviewed articles in these areas. Adekemi Taylor, PhD VP Regional Lead USA, Division 1, Quantitative Science Services Adekemi specializes in in pharmacometric strategy and analyses (including population PK, PK/PD, efficacy and safety exposure-response, and concentration-QTc modeling) to support regulatory filings, study design, and general drug development. title: Applications Open for 2027-29 New York Times Editing Residency
summary: The New York Times has opened applications for its Editing Residency, a one-of-a-kind program aimed at cultivating the next generation of editors. Editing remains a vital newsroom skill that requires…
body_text: The New York Times is now accepting applications for editing residents. The deadline to apply is Sept. 8. Read more below from the Early Career Programs team. The New York Times has opened applications for its Editing Residency , a one-of-a-kind program aimed at cultivating the next generation of editors. Editing remains a vital newsroom skill that requires practice and guidance, as well as a mastering of judgment, clarity and context. Moreover, the art of editing continues to evolve as newsrooms tell stories in increasingly creative and visual ways. Residents work full time for two years across a range of desks in the newsroom. They are paid, receive benefits and attend dedicated training and speaker programs at The Times. We plan to welcome three new residents early next year. The most competitive candidates will have at least two but no more than seven years of professional journalism experience and demonstrate a commitment to the craft of editing. Our goal is to recruit candidates of diverse backgrounds and give them the tools and experiences they need to help shape journalism. The deadline to submit an application is 5 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday, Sept. 8, after which the program directors and editors across the newsroom will collaborate to select the residents. The new residents will join The Times in late January. Interested candidates can apply here . — Ted Kim, Carla Correa and Patia Braithwaite

title: Benchmarking the Agentic SOC: How we evaluate LLMs for security workflows
summary: Elastic's LLM benchmarking framework runs every model through the same security agent and data, then scores tool use blind. Rankings flip by task.
body_text: 3 August 2026 • Dhrumil Patel Benchmarking the Agentic SOC: How we evaluate LLMs for security workflows Public leaderboards can't tell you which LLM to trust in your SOC, so Elastic built an evaluation framework that grades models on the work (tool calls, execution traces, blind judging) across Agent Builder, Attack Discovery, and automatic migration. 15 min read Generative AI , Internals An agentic SOC is only as good as the model driving it. The moment you let an LLM triage an alert, hunt across your telemetry, or author a detection rule, the question stops being "is this a smart model?" and becomes something much more specific: will it pick the right skill, call the right tool in the right order, and reach the right disposition without inventing a result it never actually checked? That is not a question a general-purpose leaderboard can answer. A model can top every public benchmark and still confidently tell you a malicious loader is "clean" because it narrated a VirusTotal verdict instead of calling VirusTotal. In a SOC, that is not a rounding error. That is a missed intrusion. So we built an evaluation framework to answer the question directly. It seeds a realistic intrusion into a live Elastic deployment, drives every available model through the same set of security tasks against the same agent, captures not just what each model said but every tool it called and every parameter it passed, and then judges the results blind. This post explains how it works and why we built it the way we did. The results themselves are published and continuously updated in the Large language model performance matrix for Elastic Security . Why generic LLM benchmarks fail for agents for security Public leaderboards measure knowledge and chat quality. They ask a model to recall facts, solve a puzzle, or write a tidy paragraph. Those are real capabilities, but they are the wrong proxy for agentic security work. Inside an agent, the model is not writing prose. It is making decisions: Which skill does this task need? Alert triage and entity risk-scoring are different jobs with different tools. Which tool, with which parameters, in which order? A hash goes to VirusTotal; an on-call question goes to the schedule; a case gets opened once, with the right fields. Is the output grounded? Did the model actually run the query and read the result, or did it produce a plausible answer with an empty trace? The most dangerous failure mode in an agentic SOC is the confident, fluent, wrong answer that was never grounded in a tool call. Generic benchmarks reward exactly that, because they only see the final text. To evaluate a SOC agent honestly, you have to grade the work, not the writing. What we actually need to measure We anchored the evaluation on the concrete capabilities a security analyst relies on, most of them built-in Agent Builder skills we shipped in Elastic Security. (For the product side of that story, see our companion post on the five Agent Builder skills in Elastic Security .) That gives us seven capability categories: Category What it tests Alert analysis Triage an alert, reach the correct disposition, pull related alerts, enrich with threat intel Entity analytics Investigate hosts and users with purpose-built entity lookups and risk context Threat hunting Generate and run queries against process, file, and network telemetry to find specific artifacts Detection rules Author a working detection rule, grounded in research when asked Workflow authoring Produce a valid, executable automation workflow (verified by actually running it) Triggering workflows Call the correct backed action for the task (hash lookup, on-call, case creation) Multi-step Chain several steps in the right order, carrying findings forward without skipping or fabricating These categories deliberately straddle two levels of the agent. Alert analysis, entity analytics, threat hunting, and detection rules are built-in Agent Builder skills; workflow authoring exercises the platform workflow capability; and triggering workflows and multi-step response exercise the custom tools and the model's ability to chain them. So the suite measures both things that matter: whether the model routes to the right skill, and whether it then selects and orders the right tools. Alongside the agent suite, we run two parallel evaluations that apply the same philosophy to different tasks. One is Attack Discovery, which uses an LLM to correlate raw alerts into coherent attack narratives. The other is Automatic Migration, which uses an LLM to translate detection content from another SIEM (Splunk, QRadar, or Microsoft Sentinel) into Elastic rules. Each has its own answer key, so we grade them separately. The framework, end to end The whole system is one automated flow. Seed the right data, point every model at the same agent and the same prompts, capture the full trace of what each model did, then anonymize and judge. The design principle throughout: hold everything constant except the model. Same agent, same skills and tools, same data, same prompts. The only variable that changes between runs is which model is answering. That is what makes the comparison fair. Seeding a realistic range You cannot benchmark an investigation without something to investigate. Real product telemetry is noisy, sensitive, and non-reproducible, so we generate a synthetic intrusion instead. The scenario is the Chrysalis backdoor campaign we detailed in our earlier Attack Discovery post: a DLL side-loading attack on a Windows host, srv-win-defend-01 , where a legitimate-looking BluetoothService.exe loads a malicious log.dll . A simulator seeds the alerts, endpoint telemetry, threat-intel documents, and an on-call schedule that make the scenario coherent enough for an agent to actually work through. One methodology detail matters here. The "malicious loader" in the scenario carries the EICAR test file hash. EICAR is the industry-standard harmless test string that every antivirus engine flags as malicious by design. Using it as the stand-in loader means VirusTotal returns a stable, unambiguous "malicious" verdict on every run, we never touch real malware, and the ground truth never drifts. A correct model reports "malicious, flagged by many engines." A model that says "clean" or never calls VirusTotal is wrong, deterministically. There is a second dataset in play, a set of eight independent detection episodes producing roughly 95 alerts, which we use as the ground truth for Attack Discovery. And this is where the most important operational rule lives: The two suites need different, mutually exclusive alert data. Attack Discovery runs against the clean episodes-only index, because its answer key assumes exactly those threats are present. Agent Builder runs with the Chrysalis intrusion seeded on top, because its prompts reference Chrysalis entities. Mix them, and both answer keys become meaningless. Getting this wrong does not throw an error. It silently corrupts the results. So the harness treats the index state as a first-class step: prep the correct data, print the alert counts, and pause for an explicit go-ahead before a single model request is sent. The agent under test Every model drives the same agent: the full Elastic AI Agent, with all of Elastic Security's built-in skills enabled (alert analysis, threat hunting, entity analytics, detection-rule editing, and more), extended with five custom, workflow-backed tools from the Chrysalis scenario. Skills and tools sit side by side on the agent. The built-in skills carry the investigative capabilities, and each one, when the model reaches for it, unlocks its own underlying tools. The five custom tools below bolt on the response actions the scenario needs: Tool What it does vt.hash.lookup Analyze a file hash with VirusTotal check.on.call.schedule Query the on-call schedule for the current responder create.case Open a case in Elastic Security create.channel Create a Slack channel for incident coordination get.time Get the current time for naming and timestamps These are live tools hitting live systems, including a real Slack connector. When a model decides to open a case or spin up an incident channel, it actually happens. That is deliberate: we want to measure what the model does when the tools are real and the side effects are real, not whether it can describe calling them. Because those side effects accumulate, the harness cleans up after every call. Authored validation workflows are deleted, and any Slack channels the agent created are archived through the same connector the agent used. Cases are intentionally kept for later inspection. The agent is given a two-phase playbook in its instructions. First a confirmation phase : verify the hash on VirusTotal, hunt the logs for corroborating activity, ground the finding in research, and reach a verdict. Then a response phase , entered only when the threat is confirmed: get the time, find the on-call responder, open a case, and spin up an incident channel. It is explicitly told not to open cases or channels for benign or low-confidence findings unless asked. That structure gives every model the same operating procedure, so what we are measuring is how well each one executes it, not whether it happened to guess the workflow. The model routing is the elegant part. Every model on the deployment is exposed as an inference connector, and the converse API takes a connector_id per call. So swapping models is a one-field change. The agent, its tools, its instructions, and the data underneath it never move. The prompt matrix The suite is 21 prompts: three variants for each of the seven capabilities, all revolving around the same Chrysalis incident so the run reads like one coherent investigation rather than disconnected trivia. Prompts are written the way an analyst actually talks, and some carry attachments, the latest alert document or a detection rule to edit, so the model has real context to work from. The three variants per capability are not just repetition. They escalate the difficulty in a deliberate way: Variant A is the clear single-skill ask. The task names what it wants, and there is one obviously right tool for the job. Variant B is realistic. It reads like a real analyst request, with enough context to be actionable but no explicit instruction on which tool to reach for. Variant C is ambiguous, routing under pressure. It is underspecified or slightly misleading, so the model has to infer intent and still pick the right capability. This is where weaker models overreach or grab the wrong tool. To make the escalation concrete, here is one capability, alert analysis, across all three variants: A (clear): "Take a look at this alert and tell me what's going on. Is it something I should worry about, and what's your recommended disposition?" (latest alert attached) B (realistic): "We've got alerts firing on srv-win-defend-01. Triage what's in the alert queue for that host, are these related to the same incident, and which entities do they share?" C (ambiguous): "I'm seeing noise on srv-win-defend-01. Is this a real threat or a false positive? Pull in any threat intel that would help me decide." Same capability, escalating difficulty: A names the task and the right tool is obvious, B forces the model to infer intent from context, and C is underspecified and slightly misleading, so the model has to resist the "false positive" framing and still investigate. A few representative prompts across the other capabilities: Threat hunting: "Hunt for signs of the Chrysalis backdoor on srv-win-defend-01. Look for BluetoothService.exe execution, suspicious DLL loads, and any C2 network or DNS activity. Walk me through what you discover." Triggering workflows: "The Chrysalis loader hash is <loader-hash>. Check this hash against VirusTotal and tell me the verdict, how many engines flagged it and what threat name." Multi-step: "There's a confirmed Chrysalis incident on srv-win-defend-01. Verify the loader hash on VirusTotal, check the on-call schedule, open a critical Security case, then spin up a Slack incident channel with the on-call responder and post the case summary and top IOCs." The multi-step prompts are where models separate. They require ordering, carrying a finding from one step into the next, and knowing when not to act. One variant explicitly says "don't escalate if it's benign," which tests judgment: since the scenario is a true positive, the correct behavior is to escalate, and a model that bails out has misread the evidence. What a single LLM evaluation run looks like Before we scale to every model, it helps to watch a single prompt run end to end. The harness dispatches the prompt to the converse API, the agent routes to the right skill, and from there the work is real. It verifies the loader hash on VirusTotal, generates and runs an ES|QL hunt that turns up the corroborating events, checks the on-call schedule and resolves the responder in Slack, opens a critical case, and spins up an incident channel with the verdict and the top IOCs. Then the harness verifies the side effects and archives the channel it created. Every step, every tool call, every parameter and result, is captured as it happens. That is one prompt. A full sweep is 21 prompts against every model in the catalog, more than 500 evaluated conversations, each one recorded in full. Capturing tool traces, tokens and latency in agent workflows This is the part that makes the framework more than a chatbot bake-off. For every single call, we capture the final answer and the full execution trace: the ordered steps the agent took, each reasoning turn, each tool it invoked with the exact parameters, the tool's result, plus token usage, latency, and the conversation and round identifiers. When a task routes through a built-in skill, the trace shows the model loading that skill first and then calling the tools the skill unlocks; when it uses a custom tool like vt.hash.lookup , the call shows up directly. Either way, the tool calls are the evidence. Here is a real captured step from a triggering-workflows prompt, trimmed for length. The model was asked to verify the loader hash on VirusTotal: { "steps": [ { "type": "reasoning", "reasoning": "The user provided a file hash for the 'Chrysalis loader' and requested a VirusTotal verdict, including the number of flagging engines and the threat name. I will use the vt_hash_lookup tool to retrieve this." }, { "type": "tool_call", "tool_id": "vt.hash.lookup", "params": { "hash": "275a021b...fd0f" }, "results": [ { "last_analysis_stats": { "malicious": 65, "undetected": 3 } } ] } ], "response": { "message": "The hash was flagged by 65 engines on VirusTotal..." } } That trace is the evidence. It lets us answer the questions a final answer alone cannot: Did the model actually call vt.hash.lookup , or did it assert a verdict with no tool call? (If the latter, the answer is unsubstantiated, no matter how confident.) Did it use the purpose-built entity tools, or fall back to a generic search and invent a risk score? For threat hunting, is there an executed query in the trace, or just a claim of findings? For workflow authoring, we go one step further and capture objective ground truth. When a model writes a workflow, the harness actually creates it, enables it, runs it, and polls the execution to a terminal status. The result is not a judgment call about whether the YAML "looks right." It either validated and executed against the live system or it did not. Blind LLM evaluation: how we remove model bias from scoring Once the matrix has run, every model has produced 21 traces. Scoring them by hand, knowing which vendor produced which output, is a recipe for bias. So we anonymize first. A deterministic obfuscation step strips the model names and relabels everything Model A, Model B, Model C, and so on, consistently across every report and across both suites, so the same model wears the same label everywhere. It also scrubs identity giveaways out of the traces themselves, the connector ids and slugified vendor names that leak into things like workflow tags, while leaving legitimate vendor mentions in tool output intact. With more than two dozen models in a run, the judge, whether a human or an LLM, sees only the labels and the traces. The judging rubric grades every capability on a 1 to 10 scale and weighs two things at once: Answer quality: correctness against the ground-truth answer key, soundness of the disposition, depth, and actionability. Tool and skill selection: did the model call and use the right tool for the job, in a reasonable order, without a pile of irrelevant calls or fabricated results? And the rule that keeps the whole thing honest: No tool call, no credit. A plausible answer produced without the supporting tool calls the task required is capped at 6 out of 10, because the result is unsubstantiated. A confident wrong answer scores lower than a hedged correct one. Evidence over eloquence. Reliability is tracked separately from quality. Some attempts error out or time out; those are counted as reliability failures and excluded from the quality average rather than being silently folded in. A model that is brilliant when it works but fails a third of the time is a different proposition from one that is merely good but never falls over, and the report shows both. What this surfaces that leaderboards miss Because we grade the trace and not the prose, the framework consistently surfaces failure modes that a text-only benchmark would score as passing: Fabricated verdicts. A model asserts a hash is malicious, or benign, without ever calling VirusTotal. Fluent, confident, and unsubstantiated. Skipping purpose-built tools. For entity questions, a model leans on a generic search and invents a risk score instead of calling the entity lookups that would return the real one. Workflows that do not run. Authored YAML that reads perfectly but fails validation or execution against the live system. The prose was fine; the automation was broken. Reasoning strong, tool use weak. Some models narrate an excellent investigation plan and then do not execute it. Others quietly do exactly the right thing with minimal commentary. Only the trace tells them apart. The headline finding is not "model X wins." It is that ranking flips depending on the capability. A model that is excellent at open-ended threat-hunting reasoning can be middling at the disciplined tool selection that multi-step response demands. The right model for an agentic SOC is a per-capability decision, and this framework is what lets you make it with evidence instead of vibes. Evaluating Attack Discovery: how LLMs correlate alerts into attack narratives The Attack Discovery suite runs the same philosophy on a different task. Attack Discovery has no tools; the model works purely from the alert context it is handed. Every model gets the identical clean corpus of roughly 95 alerts, which we constructed to contain exactly eight independent intrusions, one per host, spanning macOS, Windows, and Linux and built from real, publicly documented malware families. That number, eight, is the single most important figure in the evaluation. A top-tier model produces eight clean discoveries. Weaker ones surface a fraction of them, merge distinct intrusions into one blurry narrative, or over-split a single attack into several. We grade the output on four axes, each on the same 1 to 10 scale: Coverage: how completely the eight intrusions are accounted for, penalizing both misses and threats hidden by merging. Accuracy: correct host, malware family, kill chain, and MITRE mapping, with fabrication penalized hard. Correlation quality: the right alerts grouped together, without merging separate intrusions or over-splitting one. Actionability: usable titles and summaries, a correct entity picture, and sensible risk prioritization. The guiding principle is that a clean, accurate eight beats a noisy twelve. Surfacing extra "discoveries" that are really fragments of the same attack is not thoroughness, it is noise an analyst has to untangle. As with the agent suite, latency is reported as a secondary signal and never folded into quality, because correlation speed matters operationally when Attack Discovery runs on a schedule, but a fast wrong answer is still wrong. Evaluating Automatic Migration: Using LLMs to Port Detections from Other SIEMs to Elastic The third suite leaves the agent behind entirely and evaluates a different LLM-powered capability: Automatic Migration , the feature that ports detection content from other SIEMs into Elastic such as Splunk , QRadar , and, as of 9.5 release, Microsoft Sentinel . Here the model is not calling tools in a loop, it is doing a bulk translation job, and we grade it on how faithfully it lands. We evaluated it on a Splunk package for this run; the same method applies to any supported source. The input used are real Splunk detection rules: 52 saved searches built on Sysmon and Windows event telemetry, spanning credential access, defense evasion, discovery, and persistence. Every model migrates the identical package, so the comparison is apples to apples. The wrinkle that makes this hard is macros. Splunk searches lean on reusable macros, and 33 of the 52 rules are macro-only, meaning their entire detection logic lives behind a single macro reference like sysmon_detect_dcsync_execution rather than in the search text itself. So we hand the feature both files it needs, the 52 searches and the 200 macro definitions they depend on, and a faithful migration has to resolve that nesting instead of translating the surface text. Scoring is deliberately simple and objective. Each of the 52 rules earns a score based on translation fidelity: Score Result What it means 1.0 Full translation The Elastic rule reproduces the Splunk detection end to end, with macros expanded, filters preserved, and fields correctly mapped 0.5 Partial translation The core intent is captured but with gaps, such as an unresolved macro, a dropped filter or eval, or an incomplete field mapping 0 Miss Not translated or translated into something that does not reflect the original detection Sum the per-rule points, divide by 52, and multiply by 10 to land on the same 1 to 10 scale as the other suites. The result is a single, legible number for a genuinely messy task: what fraction of a real customer's detection library would survive an automated migration, and how much of it would land clean versus need an analyst's rework. Key takeaways Grade the work, not the writing. In an agentic SOC, the tool trace is the evidence. Judging final text alone rewards the most dangerous failure mode there is: the confident, ungrounded answer. Realistic data plus ground truth is non-negotiable. A reproducible synthetic intrusion with a known answer key, and strict discipline about which dataset backs which suite, is what makes the results mean anything. Hold everything constant except the model. Same agent, same skills and tools, same prompts, one-field model routing. Fairness comes from the setup, not the scoring. Capture the whole trace. Steps, tool calls, parameters, results, tokens, latency, and objective workflow validation. You cannot diagnose a failure you did not record. Judge blind, and separate reliability from quality. Anonymize before scoring, cap unsubstantiated answers, and never average a model's crashes into its quality score. The best model is per-capability. Rankings flip across alert triage, hunting, rule authoring, and multi-step response. Evaluate for the job you are actually asking the model to do. Conclusion: Why evidence-based LLM evaluation matters for security use-cases Three suites, three very different jobs, one standard of evidence. The agent suite measures whether a model can route to the right skill and drive the right tools in the right order. Attack Discovery measures whether it can turn a wall of alerts into the true set of intrusions, no more and no fewer. Automatic Migration measures whether it can faithfully port a detection library it did not write. Because all three land on the same blind-judged, 1 to 10 scale, every new model that ships gets a complete security profile in one view: where it is strong, where it fails, and whether those failures are quality or reliability. That evidence is not academic. It is how we decide which models to put in front of security teams, and how we keep re-checking that decision as the model landscape shifts. The agentic SOC is only as trustworthy as the evidence behind the model you put in it. This framework is how we generate that evidence, so that when we say a model is ready to triage your alerts, we can show our work, and we keep the current results live in the Large language model performance matrix for Elastic Security .
